 Follow DOJ Probing Leak of High Court's Abortion Rights Draft
 Newsmax Wires Thu, November 5, 2026 at 7:42 PM UTC 3 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. (Dreamstime) The Justice Department is pursuing a criminal investigation into the leak of the Supreme Court's draft opinion overturning the constitutional right to abortion, with prosecutors issuing grand jury subpoenas and seeking information from former court employees.
 The investigation has intensified in recent weeks, The New York Times reported, citing people familiar with the inquiry. The court's internal investigation failed to publicly identify who provided the draft to Politico in 2022.
 U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro in Washington is overseeing the inquiry, which includes career prosecutors and Carlton Davis, one of her senior deputies.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement It remains unclear what criminal law prosecutors believe was violated, whether they have identified a potential suspect, or what prompted the recent increase in investigative activity.
 The inquiry concerns the disclosure of Justice Samuel Alito's draft majority opinion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization. Politico published the draft about two months before the court formally issued its decision overturning Roe v. Wade.
 President Donald Trump has repeatedly called for identifying the source of the leak.
 "That person should be found," Trump said in July.
 Dan Bongino, then the FBI's deputy director, said in May 2025 that the administration was pursuing the matter. The use of grand jury subpoenas and the expanded criminal investigation had not previously been reported, according to the Times.
 Advertisement Advertisement The investigation raises questions about both the potential basis for criminal charges and the limits of executive branch scrutiny of the judiciary.
 Michael Dorf, a constitutional law professor at Cornell University, told the Times that the Justice Department can investigate federal crimes committed at the court. But an investigation into conduct that does not constitute a crime could threaten the separation of powers, he said.
 No federal law specifically prohibits disclosing the Supreme Court's internal records, according to the report. Legal experts said prosecutors might consider statutes concerning theft of government property or disclosure of confidential government information, though applying them to the leak would be relatively novel.
 Investigators also could examine whether employees made false statements during the court's original inquiry. Employees were warned at the time that lying to the government could lead to prosecution.
 Advertisement Advertisement Chief Justice John Roberts ordered that inquiry the day after Politico published the draft. Investigators interviewed 97 court employees and clerks, who were required to sign affidavits denying responsibility for the disclosure. The justices were consulted but were not formally interviewed, the Times previously reported.
 In January 2023, the court's top security official reported that investigators could not identify the source under a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard. The report described outdated information systems and weaknesses in security practices.
 It also said online allegations targeting clerks for liberal justices remained unsubstantiated. Competing theories about the leaker's identity and motives have never been publicly established.
 Alito later told The Wall Street Journal that he had "a pretty good idea who is responsible" but lacked sufficient evidence to identify anyone publicly.
 Advertisement Advertisement Other justices have continued to call for answers.
 "We will pursue it till the end," Justice Elena Kagan told Congress in July. Justice Amy Coney Barrett, appearing alongside her, said leaks of some court materials are illegal.
 The criminal inquiry could require access to employees and confidential records concerning the justices' deliberations. It is unclear whether the court has provided records from its internal investigation or whether any justices are being interviewed.
 Several clerks who worked at the court during the Dobbs case now hold Justice Department positions.
